technique: letting one plain object carry the feeling
lesson:
Today we work on one technique: picking one small thing in a scene and giving it your full attention so it holds the mood of the whole poem. You don't name the feeling. You just look hard at one object.

Here the poem does it with "The frost on the fence rail holds its edge a while longer." It's just frost on a rail. But it carries the pause before the day starts. It does it again with "coffee going lukewarm" and "a rafter easing." Small things, watched closely.

It works because when you watch one real object, the listener watches it too. The object stays still long enough for the mood to settle on it. You feel the quiet without being told it's quiet.

Try this: pick one plain object in your scene and write three sentences about what it's doing right now. Nothing else.

The second time through, listen for how all these small things lead to the last words, "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
A crow somewhere downhill, two notes, then nothing—
the kind of call that wants an answer it won't get,
and gets the hills instead, which keep their counsel.
You stand in the cold with coffee going lukewarm
and listen past it: the small ticking of a house
settling its accounts with the night, a rafter easing,
water in a pipe remembering where it needs to go.
There's work with numbers in it waiting on the table,
the hours that add up whether you watch them or not—
but none of that has teeth out here, not yet.
The frost on the fence rail holds its edge a while longer.
A day is just a thing you walk into, one boot then the other.

The quiet before anyone needs anything is yours alone—step into it while it's still soft,

So — up!
